bet.statement: We work both directions at once, with one strategist arguing each. On the 'not equal' side the hours go to one thing: an explicit graph, given by a short rule, that is expensive to represent by a small circuit on inputs with exactly one row and one column switched on; and beside it, an exact account of what a NOT gate can save on those inputs. On the 'equal' side the hours go to the same small inputs from the other end: families where a circuit with a NOT gate is checked to be much smaller than any circuit without one, and statements for every size about how such circuits must look.
bet.why: A checked conditional row is the reason such a family matters [L-meta-12318, named by id only; its condition is known to us for no family]; and a checked row carries a bound for circuits without NOT gates over to circuits with NOT gates when the bound is large enough [L-meta-18925]. Every bound we have checked so far is far too small for either, and this page says so line by line.

lines.name: An explicit graph that is expensive on the one-row-one-column inputs
lines.chain: The link to the question would follow from a cost above a fixed threshold, at every large size, for a family whose rule is cheap to verify, through the checked conversion [L-meta-11096] and a checked conditional row [L-meta-12318, by id only]. No family is known to us to reach that threshold; that is the missing link.
lines.last_learned: Every graph we have priced is cheap. The most expensive family we have checked a floor for, as far as we have looked, needs at least 3n + 1 AND/OR gates on n a side for n from 7 (checked in Lean, L-meta-18487) and has a circuit of at most 3n + 4 ceil(sqrt n) - 9 for n from 4 (checked in Lean, L-meta-19062), well under the threshold of about 4 gates a vertex of one side. On a generated family of 8 by 8 graphs the desk's units ask for circuits smaller than ours, and many are already checked in Lean (for one graph: at most 27 gates, L-meta-19938); our own smaller hand circuits there are computed, not checked. Checked in Lean on 26 Nov: a binary encoder with negations on 2^k one-hot inputs, by AND/OR gates of fan-in two, has at least 2 * 2^k - 2k gates, for every k from 2 (L-meta-25446); this is the layer a conversion of the kind in line N1's chain pays once a side, and the bound is linear.
lines.next: The searches on the 8 by 8 family were stood down on 27 Nov. What goes on: statements for every size, written by hand with a sketch, waiting for a builder.

lines.name: What a NOT gate can save on those inputs
lines.chain: With NOT gates directly: a circuit with NOT gates of s gates gives one without them of at most 2s plus a linear term (checked in Lean, L-meta-18925), and of at most n + m + 2(s + 1)^2 with no factor two (checked in Lean, L-meta-19164, with its converse L-meta-19302). So a bound without NOT gates above about six gates a vertex of one side would follow through to circuits with NOT gates; none of our checked rows is that large, so today this line says nothing above linear size.
lines.last_learned: All circuit bounds here use fan-in at most two. The promised inputs select exactly one row and one column. For an n by m graph with both sides nonempty, a circuit with NOT gates needs at least (n - a) + (m - b) - 1 gates, where a and b are the sizes of the largest classes of equal rows and equal columns. Lean checked this as L-meta-19361. Allowing NOT gates can save a number of gates that grows with n. One family has circuits of at most 4 gates with NOT and needs exactly 2n - 1 gates without it for every n from 2 (L-meta-20572, L-meta-20573, L-meta-20574). Two further families have circuits of at most 6 gates with NOT and need at least 2n AND/OR gates for every n from 3 (L-meta-25062 with L-meta-25203, L-meta-25235 with L-meta-24999). Lean checked these bounds. For n by n graphs with n at least 3, it remains a conjecture that every AND/OR/NOT circuit of at most s gates has an AND/OR replacement of at most s + 2n - 5 gates. L-meta-19158 states the conjecture and L-meta-19159 states its negation. Lean also checked that keeping some rows and columns gives a graph with a circuit with NOT gates no larger than the original graph's (L-meta-23955). When n and m are at least 2 and there are no equal rows or columns, if no AND/OR circuit has at most n + m - 3 gates, no AND/OR/NOT circuit has at most n + m - 3 either (L-meta-25016). For every n from 3, the n by n graph joining u to v when u differs from v and (u, v) differs from (0, 1) has a checked AND/OR circuit of at most 4n - 5 gates (L-meta-25457). For one pair of complementary 8 by 8 graphs the checked upper bounds are 24 and 30 AND/OR gates (L-meta-20166, L-meta-25451). The 5 by 5 graph of mask 18092097 needs more than 9 AND/OR gates (L-meta-25471). Lean checked that some graph with both sides of size at most 6 has a fan-in-two AND/OR circuit within a budget s, but every such circuit within s fails if all its AND gates must be on only at edges (L-meta-25474). L-meta-25475 gives a graph with both sides of size at least 2 and a circuit within s in which each gate reads two earlier wires. No AND/OR circuit within s for this graph has all its AND gates on only at edges. These are existence results. For any n by m graph with n + m at least 3, a circuit correct on the promised inputs gives one correct on all inputs for the 2-slice function at a cost of at most 6(n + m) additional gates, with NOT gates (L-meta-25462) and for AND/OR circuits (L-meta-25463).
lines.next: Statements for every size with a hand sketch, as units a contributor can finish: families where one NOT gate saves about 2n gates, and bounds from below with NOT gates one gate above the count of lines read. Small graphs by certificate through our own files.

lines.name: Bounds from below with NOT gates, by a certificate checked inside Lean
lines.chain: With NOT gates directly, at small sizes only. A bound of this kind on one graph is a fact about that graph; a statement for every size would follow only from an argument, which this line does not have.
lines.last_learned: Checked in Lean, by our own proof files sent through the public checker: no circuit with NOT gates of at most 5 gates represents one 4 by 4 graph (L-meta-19337); none of at most 9 represents the complement of the 5 by 5 matching (L-meta-17200), one size of a row checked for every N (L-meta-17187).
lines.next: The same for more small graphs, cut into pieces small enough for one proof file.

lines.name: One candidate rule for line N1, attacked from above
lines.chain: Through line N1 only: if this rule's graphs were expensive at every size, the statement of N1 would follow. We have no bound from below for it at all.
lines.last_learned: Circuits far under the plain size are checked in Lean at two sizes (a 32 by 32 graph: at most 207 gates, L-meta-19034; a 128 by 128 graph: at most 2046 gates, L-meta-19035). By our own counts (computed, not checked) the rule lacks a property we wanted an argument to use. Checked in Lean since: for the 32 by 32 graph of the rule, circuits with NOT gates allowed of at most 190 and at most 180 gates (L-meta-19143, L-meta-20578), and an AND/OR circuit of at most 224 gates (L-meta-17144). Computed, not checked (27 Nov): AND/OR circuits of 204 and 201 gates for the same graph, by letting one AND serve two of the rule's rectangles. On paper, not checked (27 Nov, four seats): written in its starting state the rule is local round by round, and a version of it with fewer rounds than about a fifth of the number of bits in one name (three rounds excepted) would have circuits far under the size the chain's condition asks for; the rule as it stands uses about half the number of bits in one name in rounds, and between those two we hold neither an attack nor a statement.
lines.next: The gap in rounds between about a fifth and a half of the number of bits in one name: an attack from the equal bench first; three statements about the low-round versions wait for a builder.

lines.name: Small circuits for hard families at small sizes, searched from above
lines.chain: No chain to the question is held from this line: circuits at finitely many small sizes are data, and we hold no rule for every size.
lines.last_learned: Computed, not checked (25 Nov): for 3-colourability and Hamiltonian cycle at 4, 5 and 6 vertices our plain rules grow about six-fold a vertex; at 4 vertices the least circuit found for Hamiltonian cycle with NOT gates allowed uses no NOT gate. Nothing here is checked in Lean as a bound from below. (Figures as in plan/MAP.md, section B, rows B5 and B8.)
lines.next: Not staffed today. It reopens on a rule that beats the six-fold growth at two consecutive sizes.

lines.name: Two copies for less than twice one
lines.chain: None to the question. It is a measure of sharing: a circuit for two disjoint copies of a graph that is cheaper than two circuits shows gates serving both copies.
lines.last_learned: Checked in Lean: two disjoint 4 by 4 crowns are represented with at most 21 AND/OR gates (L-meta-17170) while one needs at least 11 (L-meta-8977). Which gates serve both copies has not been read.

lines.name: Where a NOT gate begins to pay for a function with a fast algorithm
lines.chain: None to the question. It is a control: it says whether tables at the sizes we can solve are able to show an algorithm's cancellation at all.
lines.last_learned: Checked in Lean: the 2 by 2 Boolean matrix product has no circuit of at most 11 AND, OR and NOT gates (L-meta-11868). Computed, not checked: bipartite perfect matching at 2 by 2 costs 3 gates with or without NOT. (As in plan/MAP.md, section B, row B6.)
lines.next: Not staffed today; its question moved to line N2, where the saving is checked for every n from a small size on.

ruled_out.how: Our own circuits cap them: the crown has a circuit of about 3n gates (checked in Lean, L-meta-19062), under the threshold; a proposed floor of 4n - 6 on that second family was refuted (checked in Lean, L-meta-18140).

ruled_out.what: Tables of exact sizes at up to nine inputs as a way to see a hard graph
ruled_out.how: No entry at a size we can compute can reach the threshold of line N1; the tables were kept as data and no longer extended as a line of work.

ruled_out.what: Lowering the conversion's own overhead as a line of work
ruled_out.how: It would move the threshold by a constant factor and give nothing by itself; stood down by both strategists.

ruled_out.what: Three earlier bets: a crossing argument on the plane's point-line graph; the exact size of the Petersen graph's edge function with NOT gates; a counting lemma on arcs
ruled_out.how: The plane's graph has a cheap rule, so the checked conversion caps it; the Petersen units were handed back by searchers for hours without an answer and were withdrawn; the arc lemma priced a class of circuits we already held. No seat worked on any of the three on 26 November.

ruled_out.what: Three notions tried as predictors of cost and dropped the hour they were tested
ruled_out.how: Computed, not checked: the number of rectangles covering a graph's complement does not predict what a NOT gate saves; the drop in cost when one line is deleted never stays above 3 as a 4 by 4 graph grows; a row-column symmetry of the 8 by 8 family does not go with smaller circuits.

ruled_out.what: Bounds from below with NOT gates at 6 gates and over on 4 by 4 graphs, as one proof file a contributor could send
ruled_out.how: Measured on our own certificates (computed): about 5 MB at 6 gates and about ten times that at 7, against a limit of 512 KiB a library file. The 5-gate cases went through as our own files (checked in Lean: L-meta-19337, L-meta-19493).

ruled_out.what: A break of the conjecture L-meta-19158 at side 4
ruled_out.how: Computed, not checked: one solver call each on five of the six classes with AND/OR cost 11 found no circuit with NOT gates of at most 7 gates; one complete enumeration found none of 6 on any class with AND/OR cost 10. One class at 11 was not asked.

ruled_out.what: The number of rectangles covering the complement as a predictor of what a NOT gate saves
ruled_out.how: Dropped by its own table test the hour it was tried (computed).

ruled_out.what: A system of gadgets for exact matching as a road to a reduction
ruled_out.how: Computed and re-counted by a second seat (25 Nov): the fan-out gadget found has mixed states on both sides of the target count, so copies can cancel; stood down the same evening.

ruled_out.what: A small decomposition of one explicit tensor below a threshold, as a search for contributors
ruled_out.how: Computed twice, not checked: the threshold lies below the tensor's own side at every size a witness could be written, so no finite witness exists in reach.

ruled_out.what: Three readings of what a NOT gate at the top of a circuit saves: a fixed toll added to the cheaper circuit, the cheaper circuit turned over, and one hand construction of ours
ruled_out.how: Computed, not checked: read from every least circuit we hold for the 4 by 4 graphs where a graph and its complement differ most and where they cost the same; the dearer circuit shares almost no gate with the cheaper one, and the gate kinds do not swap.

ruled_out.what: Any count made on the one-row-one-column inputs (reads of inputs, rectangles, wires that mix rows with columns) as a way past two gates a line on each side
ruled_out.how: On paper, with two checked rows behind it (L-meta-25462, L-meta-25463): a circuit on these inputs is within a linear allowance of a circuit for the edge rule on all inputs, and every graph has a circuit that gathers the name bits at about two gates a line a side; so past that the question is the size of circuits for the rule itself.

would_change_the_bet: An explicit graph, at any one size, whose cost on these inputs is checked above 4 gates a vertex of one side: line N1 would get all the hours.
A checked row saying a NOT gate can save more than 2n - 5 on some family (the conjecture L-meta-19158 refuted): line N2 would turn to how large the saving can grow.
Circuits for the candidate rule of line N4 that keep shrinking at both sizes: the candidate is struck and N1 needs another.
Any checked row from the equal side that gives small circuits for a family this side hoped was hard.

A checked proof of L-meta-19158: on these inputs a NOT gate would then be capped at a saving that grows only linearly, and the equal side's hours would move to functions where a NOT gate must do more.
A unit asking for a smaller circuit on an NP-complete family that is met at two consecutive sizes under our growth rate: line E1 would reopen with all the equal side's hours.

bets.statement: On the 'not equal' side the hours go to one thing: an explicit graph, given by a short rule, that is expensive to represent by a small circuit on inputs with exactly one row and one column switched on; and beside it, an exact account of what a NOT gate can save on those inputs.
bets.why:
A computer program can be drawn as a circuit: a network of tiny steps, each combining two earlier values. If some puzzle
whose answers are easy to check needed circuits that grow enormously as the puzzle grows, then, by a step not yet checked here,
finding answers would be harder than checking them. We do not know how to show that for any real puzzle. So we work where everything can be
counted exactly: small grids of yes and no, built from the simplest steps, with and without the one step that flips yes to
no. We want to learn, gate by gate, what makes a grid expensive, and whether the flipping step can ever save more than a
little.

bets.would_change:
- A grid given by a short rule that is checked in Lean to need clearly more steps than every rule-given grid we have
  priced so far. All our hours would move to that family.
- A checked proof that the flipping step never saves more than about two steps for each row of the grid (today a conjecture on our desk,
  L-meta-19158, with its opposite beside it). Then circuits with that step need no separate study on these inputs.
- A checked example where the flipping step saves far more than that. Then counting steps without it tells us little
  about circuits with it, and we stop trying to carry bounds from one kind to the other.
- Three more looks at small grids that each end where tonight's did: in an idea our own record already held. Then we
  leave small grids for a different object.

bets.statement: On the 'equal' side the hours go to the same small inputs from the other end: families where a circuit with a NOT gate is checked to be much smaller than any circuit without one, and statements for every size about how such circuits must look.
bets.why:
If P equals NP, the answer is a thing you can hold: a fast method for a hard problem. So this side searches,
and it searches where a search can be finished and checked: very small circuits, the simplest model of a computation. Today it
studies one switch, the NOT gate. On our inputs, with exactly one row and one column switched on, we can work out exactly how
much smaller a circuit gets when that switch is allowed, and for several families Lean has checked that a single NOT gate saves
a number of gates that keeps growing with the size. We measure such savings where they can be measured exactly.

  L-meta-19158, on the desk with its opposite beside it). This place would then be measured out, and the side would move to inputs
  where a NOT gate has to do more.
- A checked circuit that breaks that conjecture. We would study that one circuit before anything else.
- A search for smaller circuits for a hard problem that succeeds at two sizes in a row faster than our own rules grow. That search
  is stood down today (line E1 of the plan); it would reopen with all of this side's hours.
- A night in which our tables, at the sizes we can finish, show nothing they did not show the night before. Tables at small sizes
  are data, not an argument; when they stop showing anything we stop adding to them.
bets.last_link: No chain to the question is held on this side: circuits at finitely many small sizes are data, and we hold no rule for every size.
